To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
an odor paired with CCK octapeptidelater inhibits feeding in neonatal rat pups.
an odor paired with injections of the satiating hormone CCK octapeptide in neonatal rats later inhibits intake when the odor is presented alone.
the CCKA antagonist devazepide, given before an odor paired with a meal, blocks the later ability of that odor to inhibit feeding in the rat.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of CCK as a satiety hormone.
how the taste of a food influences its intake and the development of food preferences.
how an animal learns to associate a food with a stimulus that is not food, and how this learning affects subsequent behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the conditioned odor inhibits intake by sensitizing a CCKA receptor system.
the conditioned odor inhibits independent feeding in the neonatal rat through a CCKA receptor-dependent mechanism.
the CCKA antagonist devazepide blocks the conditioned odor's ability to reduce feeding in the presence of a food reward.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the odor is a conditioned stimulus that inhibits intake by acting through the CCKA system.
CCK is a potent unconditioned and conditioned satiety signal.
the odor is paired with a CCKA receptor mediated event and that this pairing causes the odor to later inhibit feeding by enhancing CCKA receptor function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the conditioned stimulus is not necessarily an effective unconditioning stimulus, but it is an effective unconditionally effective unconditioning.

CCK is a powerful unconditioned stimulus that is effective even when the animal does not eat during the conditioning process, and that the conditioned stimulus can change the processing of CCH by the CCKA receptors.
CCK can be a very effective unconditioned reinforcer in neonatal rats, and that an odor that is paired with CCK can later inhibit feeding in neonatal animals that are not food or matrenally deprived.
